title: Steiner's Theorem: The Cost of an Off-Centre Axis
topic: Parallel-axis (Steiner's) theorem — I = I_cm + Md², the moment of inertia about any axis equals the inertia about a parallel axis through the centre of mass plus M times the squared offset

beats.narration: We know a disk's moment of inertia is one half M R squared, about its centre. But what if you spin it about a different axis?

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-top
Same disk — different axis. Does the inertia change?

beats.narration: Take the same disk with two parallel axes — one through the centre of mass, and one offset by a distance d. Spinning about the offset axis is always harder. But how much harder?

elements.content: Left: disk centred, faint amber fill, amber rim. Rotating about its centre at constant ω.
Left axis cross + 'CM' label at disk centre
Left caption: 'about the centre'
Right: same disk, but pinned at offset axis at distance d from CM. Whole disk swings about the pin; CM traces a circle of radius d.
Right axis cross at offset pin + 'P' label
Dashed segment from pin to CM with d label
Faint dashed circle of radius d showing the path of the CM
Right caption: 'about an axis offset by d'
Spinning off-centre is always harder — the centre itself has to swing.

beats.narration: Steiner's theorem says the total inertia equals I about the centre of mass, plus M times d squared. The first term is the body still spinning about its own centre. The second term is the centre itself swinging in a circle of radius d.

elements.content: I = I_cm + Md²
spin about its own centre
centre carried around the pin
Tiny amber disk glyph (with rotation tick) — illustrates I_cm term
Tiny rose dot orbiting a pin at radius d — illustrates Md² term

beats.narration: Take a disk spun about its rim, where d equals R. Then I equals one half M R squared, plus M R squared, giving three halves M R squared — three times the inertia of spinning about the centre.

elements.content: Disk pinned at the rim (right edge). Pin marked. Dashed radius from pin to centre labelled d = R.
Pin axis cross + 'P' label at rim
d = R label on dashed line from pin to centre
I_rim = ½MR² + MR²
I_rim = ³⁄₂ MR²
About the rim → 3× the inertia about the centre.

beats.narration: The centre of mass always gives the smallest moment of inertia. Move the axis away, and spinning only gets harder.

elements.content: Parabolic curve: I as a function of axis offset d, with minimum at d = 0 (the centre of mass)
Marker at minimum showing I = I_cm at d = 0
The centre of mass minimises the moment of inertia.
